Stage 4 · Grammar

Saying how likely something is

The future forms of the last two lessons carry the event. These structures carry your confidence in it.

1 · Look at these lines from the recording.
From the listening
  • a  I wouldn’t be surprised if it happened.
  • b  I still doubt people would be satisfied with a virtual holiday.
  • c  I expect they’ll just travel more within their own countries.
  • d  I think it’s bound to happen.
  • e  There’s no chance of me eating something like that.
  • f  Well, yes, I suppose it might happen.
2 · Answer the three questions about the lines above.

3 · Read the table.
StructureHow likelyExample
be bound to + infinitivealmost certainPrices are bound to rise again next year.
be sure to + infinitivealmost certainThat is sure to happen within a decade.
be likely to + infinitiveprobableHalf these jobs are likely to disappear.
will probably / probably won’tprobableThey will probably travel at home instead. She probably won’t apply.
I expect / I doubt (+ clause)probable / improbableI expect they will. I doubt people would be satisfied.
might / may / couldpossibleIt might happen, but nobody has built one yet.
there is no chance of + -ingimpossible, in the speaker’s viewThere is no chance of that happening here.
I would not be surprised if + pastpossible, held at a distanceI wouldn’t be surprised if it happened.

Two patterns do most of the damage in exams. Likely, bound and sure take to + infinitive; chance, possibility and hope take of + -ing. And probably changes places around the negative: will probably not and probably won’t.

4 · One prediction, five degrees of confidence.
Printed food is bound to arrive within ten years.  →  almost certain.
Printed food is likely to arrive within ten years.  →  probable.
Printed food might arrive within ten years.  →  possible, no more.
I doubt printed food will arrive that quickly.  →  improbable.
There is no chance of printed food arriving that quickly.  →  impossible, in my view.
1 · Read the explanation.
The event, and your confidence in it

The future forms you met in lessons 17 and 18 say what happens and when. This lesson adds the second layer: how sure you are. In careful English the two are kept apart, which is why a single sentence can carry a strong prediction and a weak commitment at the same time — it will probably happen, although I doubt it will happen here.

The strong end. Be bound to and be sure to both take an infinitive and both mean “almost certainly”: prices are bound to rise. Note that bound here has nothing to do with obligation. The middle. Be likely to + infinitive is the neutral choice for probable, and will probably does the same work with a different structure. I expect and I doubt introduce a clause and put the confidence in the reporting verb rather than in the prediction itself.

The weak end. Might, may and could mean possible and commit you to nothing. There is no chance of + -ing is the strongest denial available, and it is a statement about the speaker’s belief, not about the world. I would not be surprised if + past tense is a useful halfway house: the past form after if makes the event hypothetical without making it unlikely.

What follows what. likely / bound / sure → to + infinitive. chance / possibility / hope → of + -ing. expect / doubt / suppose → a clause. Getting the pattern wrong is more noticeable than choosing slightly the wrong strength.

Word order and negatives
  • She will probably apply.  ·  She probably won’t apply. — the adverb moves.
  • It is unlikely to happen is more natural than it is not likely to happen.
  • There is little chance of it happening — weaker than no chance, stronger than some chance.
  • I doubt it will happen — English puts the negative in doubt, not in the clause after it.

Two things to watch

1 — Likely is an adjective, not an adverb. It will likely happen is common in North American writing but is best avoided here; use it is likely to happen or it will probably happen.

2 — Do not double the hedge. It is bound to probably happen and I doubt it will not happen both collapse. Choose one structure and let it carry the whole of your confidence.

11 · Read this before the extra practice.
A scale, and the grammar each rung takes

These structures do not describe the event; they describe your confidence about it. From the top: be bound to and be sure to (almost certain) → be likely to, will probably, I expect (probable) → might, may, could, I suppose it might (possible) → be unlikely to, probably won’t, I doubt (improbable) → there is no chance of (impossible, in your view).

The forms that follow them are fixed, and getting them wrong is what marks a B2 answer down: be bound / sure / likely / unlikely to + infinitive · might / may / could + bare infinitive · there is no chance / little chance of + -ing · I expect / I doubt + a clause · I wouldn’t be surprised if + past tense, which sounds odd until you see that the past here marks distance, not time.

Where the negative goes, and how confident you sound

English usually puts the negative on the confidence, not the event. I don’t think it will happen is normal; I think it won’t happen is possible but heavier. Similarly, She probably won’t apply and She is unlikely to apply are the usual ways to say it, not she is likely not to apply.

Register matters in a written argument. Bound to and no chance of are strong and personal, and a reader can push back on them; likely to, unlikely to and I would not be surprised if are defensible and are what essay writers reach for. Hedging is not weakness here: it is what makes a claim survive a challenge.

Errors to watch: It is bound happen → bound to happen · There is no chance to happen → no chance of that happening · It might to happen → might happen · I doubt that it will not work — a double negative that says the opposite of what you mean · I wouldn’t be surprised if it will happen → if it happened.

4 · Read the model essay.
Model · a balanced opinion essay

Whether the office survives the next twenty years is not really a question about technology, which has already settled it, but about what employers believe they lose when they cannot see their staff. Both answers have serious arguments behind them, and neither is as obvious as the people arguing for it usually claim.

The case for the end of the office is largely economic. Companies in every large city are running out of space and are unwilling to buy more, and the work that once required a desk now requires a connection. The generation now entering employment has never known anything else, so the habit is bound to spread simply because the people who find it strange are retiring. On this reading, the office is likely to become a place people visit for two or three days rather than somewhere they go.

The case against it is about trust rather than equipment. Businesses want visibility of what is being produced, and a manager who cannot see the work being done tends to assume it is not. There is also work that genuinely needs a room and other people in it, and I doubt any amount of software will change that. Some employers will probably use technology to watch people more closely rather than to free them.

On balance the first view seems more likely to me, although not in the strong form it is usually stated in. I would not be surprised if the office of 2045 looked much like the office of today, with the same desks and half the people in them on any given morning. There is no chance of the building disappearing altogether; what is disappearing is the assumption that everybody has to be inside it at nine.
